newsitem.title: UK: Dlr higher at Euro close, still eyeing 1.60 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr higher at Euro close, still eyeing 1.60 marks.

text.p: The dollar closed higher against the mark in Europe, boosted by short-covering after its brief decline below 1.59 marks, traders said.
Comments by Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp helped to push the dollar up in a market still keen to see it move into higher ground above 1.60 marks.
Krupp, a dove on the council, said German jobless figures released last week showed the economy was in a grave state and the Bundesbank could not ignore this.
Against the yen the dollar weakened to below 117 yen, undermined by a slide in the mark/yen cross, dealers said.

"There was a good opportunity to buy the dollar at lower levels, and the Krupp comments served as a good excuse for the market to push the dollar higher," Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets said.
At 1545 GMT the dollar was at 1.5940/45 marks and 116.55/60 yen compared with 1.5912/22 and 117.16/26 in late Europe on Wednesday.
Mark/yen was at 73.12/15, down from 73.65/68. The mark's decline accelerated after it fell through key support at 73.55, which set it on target to fall below 73, traders said.
"There's a top forming process on the dollar majors, and the dollar has to set new highs today to change that picture," said Spain.
As long as dollar/mark stayed below 1.6000/20 it was at risk of a deeper correction. On dollar/yen, a break above 117.40/60 would be needed for the dollar to accelerate higher, he said.
Dealers also noted vague talk that the Bank of England sold dollars for yen on behalf of the Bank of Japan in European trading.
"There is some concern that the BOJ might be returning to the market," a dealer at a Swiss bank said.

Sterling lost about half a pfennig after news that a member of parliament of the UK's ruling Conservative Party died. The death of Iain Mills means the Conservatives are clearly in a minority in parliament.

Strong UK retail prices and the lack of a rate rise after Wednesday's monetary meeting between Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George also added to the pound's weaker tone, dealers said.
The pound was at 2.6676/86 marks, compared with 2.6693/03 at the previous European close. Sterling/dollar was at $1.6751/59 from $1.6775/85.
The mark was under attack again from the Norwegian crown, which made a new high at 3.9720 per mark, the highest since September 1992. Mark/crown was at 3.9729/54 versus 3.9970/90.

The German currency also lost ground against the peseta after the Bank of Spain surprised with a cut in its key money market rate by 25 basis points to 6.00 percent. Mark/peseta was at 83.47/52 from 83.69/71.

The French franc showed little reaction to the Bank of France's decision to keep its key intervention rate unchanged at 3.25 percent. Most analysts had expected a cut. Mark/Paris was at 3.3745/50 versus 3.3752/55.
Rumours the Bank of Japan might have left sell orders above 117.50 yen weighed on the dollar's upside, traders said.

The dollar showed little response to the latest round of official Japanese jawboning overnight. Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka called wild foreign exchange fluctuations, and specifically excessive yen depreciation, undesirable.
Dollar sentiment remained bullish but analysts noted the U.S. unit needed a fresh stimulus to extend its rally.
"We are on reversal watch across the board (on the dollar)," said Darren Spain, global foreign exchange analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston.
-- Astrid Zweynert +44 171 5427792
